prose.def: To freely give or bestow something as a favor, to release or hand over a person, or to graciously forgive sins or wrongs.

In the Byzantine New Testament's 23 uses, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "forgive" nearly half the time (10×, 48%), with the rest spread across giving, granting, and bestowing — so the word covers both freely handing over a gift and freely pardoning a debt or sin. The everyday papyri capture this warmth nicely: one writer says that if you grant his request, "I shall be eternally obliged to you," showing how giving and showing kindness blur together. Lexicons note the "forgive" sense is a later Greek development (like the Latin condonare).
prose.caution: The senses overlap heavily — even the lexicons admit "show kindness" and "freely bestow" can hardly be separated — so the dividing lines between forgive, give, and grant are softer than the counts suggest.

prose.def: A person who guides someone helpless or blind by taking their hand and leading them.
senseLabels: one who leads a helpless person by the hand
prose.article: χειραγωγός literally combines "hand" and "lead," meaning a guide who takes a helpless or blind person by the hand. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 13:11, where the blinded sorcerer Elymas seeks people to lead him around. The lexicons (Abbott-Smith, Dodson, Strong's) agree closely on this sense, and Moulton-Milligan confirm the word and its relatives turn up in everyday Koine papyri, including a London papyrus pairing it with words for gentleness.

prose.def: A handwritten document, especially a signed record of debt or a legal bond.
prose.article: χειρόγραφον literally means something written by hand, but in everyday usage it had narrowed to a specific legal sense: a signed IOU or bond recording a debt. The papyri make this concrete — one document (P Oxy IV.745) speaks of a buyer drawing up a χειρόγραφον for a wine purchase, and another asks someone to press a debtor to settle his bond. It appears just once in the New Testament (Colossians 2:14), where it is used figuratively, and the Septuagint examples in Tobit likewise refer to a written record.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and was absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single English word, so its precise force there is debated.

receipts.how: The sole NT occurrence uses χειρόγραφον figuratively for a legal bond of debt canceled by Christ, matching the definition's emphasis on a signed record of debt.

Moulton-Milligan's papyri evidence (P Oxy IV.745) corroborates the definition's core sense of a written bond or certificate of debt as the dominant documentary usage behind this verse.

prose.def: Made by human hands; describing physical objects or practices fashioned by people, often contrasted with what is divine or heavenly.
prose.article: χειροποίητος literally means "made by hands" and describes things constructed by human effort. In the New Testament it appears 6 times, mostly of physical temples (as in Mark 14:58 and Acts 7:48), and once of circumcision performed by people (Ephesians 2:11). What's striking is the shift in usage: in the Septuagint (12 times) the word is applied only to idols, often translating the Hebrew אֱלִיל, while a travel-letter papyrus from the 1st–2nd century AD uses it simply for "works of art made by hands" along the Nile.
prose.caution: The three measured sense labels reflect minor wording differences rather than truly distinct meanings; all point to the same core idea of "made by hands."

prose.def: To appoint or select someone for a role; in the NT used both for direct apostolic appointment and for election by a group, without consistently implying a formal vote.
senseLabels: selection or election by a group (2Co 8:19)
prose.article: χειροτονέω literally means to stretch out the hand, and originally described voting by raised hands in the Athenian assembly, but in everyday Koine it came to mean simply to select or appoint. It appears just twice in the New Testament (Acts 14:23 and 2 Corinthians 8:19), where it covers both appointing without a formal vote and choosing by vote. The papyri show the word still alive in ordinary administrative life — one document from A.D. 192 has a man who "nominated himself" for the urgent office of cosmetes.
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a broad range spanning formal voting to plain appointment, the precise sense in any given verse is hard to pin down.
